speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This year marks the 75th Anniversary of the fall of Singapore in World War II.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The events in the 20 years since that day have marked the tumultuous journey of Singapore to Independence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even after Independence, security became one of our concerns and National Service (NS) started shortly after.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This year, we also celebrate the 50th Anniversary of NS.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Happily, Singapore has grown against the backdrop of domestic peace and prospered.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: China has responded by continuing its security patrols and even sailing its aircraft carrier through the region.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While I think conflict is not in either party's interest, the threat certainly seems to be looming amongst the great powers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Meanwhile, terror threats that have captured our imagination in recent years continue.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even as the so-called Islamic State loses ground in Iraq and Syria, the terror attacks continue.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Last year, these included attacks in Nice, Yemen, Turkey and Bangladesh, with the death tolls in the hundreds.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some of these were organised attacks, while others were lone wolf attacks by self-radicalised individuals.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This makes the reach of terrorism far and wide, with lone wolf attacks being particularly difficult to detect.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the region, too, not all appears comfortable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Indonesia, for the first time in many years, was wrecked by violent demonstrations in Jakarta in response to remarks made by its governor.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But physical threats are not the only threats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Cyberattacks, I think, are a threat that has captured our imagination for a long time but now it seems to have come very close to home.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The security threats we face come from far, wide, in many forms, and MINDEF is very much in the frontline to deal with many of these.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For this reason, I would like to open this debate by asking what MINDEF sees as the most salient security challenges facing Singapore today, both conventional and unconventional.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: This agreement allows the US access to facilities on a rotational basis without bringing up sensitive sovereignty issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Singapore's sophisticated facilities and political standing in the region allows us to host the US thus.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: In recent times, much change and transformation are shaping up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: These include the newly elected US President and also a rising China, with certain observable characteristics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Trump's administration leaves a lot of uncertainties on outcomes in these relations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: The leadership in both countries is becoming more unpredictable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Whilst China wants to exercise influence, the US stand is also unclear and in limbo.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: What is MINDEF's view of this complex, transitional issue, which will have implications on our security and growth, both regionally and globally?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Are there anticipated changes expected in our defence relations with the US and China, knowing that maintaining strong relations is important for us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Today, besides traditional security issues, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is confronted with complex, non-traditional threats, namely, in the form of terrorism and transnational crimes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: These may include trafficking, money laundering, cybercrimes and even people smuggling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: The region is also not exempt from threats of nuclear weapons as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: A closer and stronger cooperation and alignment is necessary, bilaterally as well as with our multilateral partnerships and an understanding must continue to be inculcated and strengthened.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: How is Singapore working with our ASEAN partners and others in the region in the areas of, firstly, conflict prevention, mitigation and mediation; secondly, counter terrorism and transnational crimes curbing; and thirdly, peacekeeping activities and operations, including maritime security?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A month earlier, the latest in a long series of the Semangat Bersatu joint military exercises between the Malaysian and Singaporean armies was successfully concluded.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While it remains important to remember that such exercises were halted when relations turn sour in the past, the reality of the geopolitical environment today emphasises the importance of greater defence cooperation and not less, so as to improve bilateral and regional security.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, is the Ministry considering the introduction of newer confidence-building initiatives with both Malaysia and Indonesia, in addition to the Malacca Straits patrol, the Five Power Defence Arrangement (FPDA) and the ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting (ADMM) and ADMM-Plus frameworks?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In previous cuts, I have suggested pursuing the prospects of joint peacekeeping initiatives and training for international assignments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is the Ministry considering newer areas for military-to-military cooperation with Malaysia, beyond those like the Semangat Bersatu exercise series, so as to take advantage of the goodwill arising out of the political relationship with a view to more durable ties in future?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In contrast, while the political relationship with Indonesia is more complex, as a result of the politically diverse and more representative democratic terrain today, the military relationship appears to be an all-weather one despite occasional political turbulence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As Members would remember, DCA was linked to an extradition treaty between both countries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: All this resulted in a package agreement that was stillborn.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Amrin Amin, you have two cuts, please take them together.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: As a multiracial and multi-religious country, disinformation campaigns and fake news can erode trust among various groups, and this can be exploited by external parties.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Minister Ng Eng Hen had also warned in 2013 that some types of false news could have exponential consequences which could undermine our national security.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Online misinformation could spread widely during tense or volatile situations, causing confusion and chaos which could weaken the community's resolve and cause disunity.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: How is MINDEF preparing to respond to such threats in the information domain?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Last year, Minister Ng talked about the "troubled peace" that we will face in an increasingly volatile and borderless environment.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: We have witnessed recently alleged state-directed hybrid attacks which combine conventional and unofficial military means with cyber warfare, propaganda and indirect tactics.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: How prevalent are such attacks in our region and are we vulnerable?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: What can be done to guard Singapore against such attacks?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Beyond conventional war, there are areas, including terrorism, cybersecurity, pandemic management, humanitarian assistance and disaster relief.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The year 2016 alone has seen a wide spate of terror attacks around the world.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The unveiling of this foiled terrorist attack highlighted the real possibility of future terrorist attacks in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The training syllabus of National Servicemen (NSmen) and full-time National Servicemen (NSFs), as some of us know it, was largely based on conventional armed conflict.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Specifically, I would like to ask the Minister if MINDEF has put in sufficient preparations such that our Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) personnel are trained for roles in counterterrorism and are equipped with the necessary intelligence, skillsets, technology and equipment to deal with terrorism.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: More importantly, in the event of an attack in Singapore, are our servicemen trained to deal with its aftermath?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Indeed, is our population prepared to deal with such an aftermath and relief efforts?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Cybersecurity, as others have pointed out, is also particularly important to Singapore because our vision is to become an even smarter city.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The recent breach of our I-net system clearly illustrated our vulnerability and showed us how hard it is to defend against determined hackers.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Cyber terrorism can also potentially cripple us in Singapore as we leverage the Internet and conduct increasingly a large part of our daily lives on the Net.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister how MINDEF and other Government agencies, such as the Cyber Security Agency (CSA), GovTech and so on, are preparing to strengthen our cybersecurity, and what measures are in place to mitigate the damage if breached?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Chairman, in the Mumbai terrorist bombing incident not too long ago, the use of mobile telephones and electronic devices featured strongly in the coordination and execution phases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Cyberattacks are, indeed, growing in volume by the day and pose very complex and unique challenges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: The emergence of sophisticated information systems has, indeed, transformed the world we live in today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Cyber threats do not fit in readily into the traditional security framework that exists in most modern states today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: New approaches are crucial and the appropriate and balanced role of the military is central to this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: The military response is not the only response but part of a concerted and consolidated approach, including legal and political responses and so on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: How is MINDEF approaching this issue and also how is it being coordinated with other agencies in Singapore, such as the law enforcement agencies that we have here?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: How does this framework fit into our national cybersecurity ecosystem?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the pervasive revolution we are experiencing, technology is pervasive and impacting many aspects of our work and life.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Unlike previous industrial revolutions, the Fourth Industrial Revolution is evolving at an exponential pace.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This revolution is characterised by the emergence of a range of technologies fusing the physical, digital and biological worlds, creating new ways in which technology is immersed in our lives.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These include technological breakthroughs in artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, the Internet of Things, autonomous vehicles, 3D printing, nanotechnology and quantum computing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We know that technology enables possibilities and it is an important part of MINDEF's transformation effort to build the next-generation SAF.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But the differentiator is not just technology but how technology is used.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In his speech marking the 50th Anniversary of DTC, President Tony Tan described DTC as standing at the forefront of scientific and engineering discovery.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: DTC pioneers have played a key role in shaping Singapore's defence technology.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can the Minister share how MINDEF is tapping on these emerging technologies in support of Singapore's defence?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Apart from leveraging technology, how is MINDEF engaging its talent base to build the capacity and capabilities to realise the potential of these emerging technologies?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, drones are becoming more common and sophisticated.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They will grow to be an integral part of our lives due to their many useful applications, from logistics to transport, photography, videos and even patrols.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But in the wrong hands, they can be a threat to our national security.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They can be launched from almost anywhere and once they are airborne, they can reach any location within a few kilometres in minutes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The smaller ones are almost undetectable in flight.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Current radar systems are designed to track larger aircrafts.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For those with bad intentions, such items may include poisonous powders or gases like sarin, incendiary devices, grenades and bombs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: More worrying, it can be very difficult to trace the owner and operator of a drone.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The risk of detection during the process of transporting, launching and operating one is low.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is MINDEF's assessment of the threat drones pose to Singapore now and in the future?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What measures does the Ministry have to ensure our national security will not be compromised with the increasingly widespread use of drones in our daily lives and in the near future?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: As a small country, technology is going to be fundamental to our defence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: What is equally important is developing our own technology.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I have personally seen how important these changes can be.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I was in a group of NSmen that did NS with the M-16.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Later on in reservist, I was acquainted with the SAR-21, a wholely modified weapon.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I have also seen the wonderful difference this makes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I used to barely pass my shooting tests when I was in NS.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: With the SAR-21, my entire section became marksmen.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: So, there is tremendous improvement in productivity with our homegrown weapons.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: What is MINDEF doing to ensure that we have enough people with background in STEM to ensure that we will maintain our own capabilities to develop such technology?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Over the years, we have continually modernised SAF which gave rise to the Second Generation SAF in the 1980s and 1990s.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: This transformation journey upgraded our systems to becoming an advanced networked force with leading-edge capabilities.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Today, the threats facing Singapore have, indeed, expanded.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: SAF remains more important than ever to defend Singapore against a broad array of such threats.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: How would SAF do more with less manpower available to it?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: How have we leveraged on technologies, as Mr Vikram Nair has spoken about, to improve our productivity, combat effectiveness and, of course, expand the number of marksmen?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Can the Minister provide an overview of the SAF's capabilities and readiness on land, at sea and in the air, and, indeed, in space through satellites, to effectively defend Singapore against such a broad array of threats?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Indeed, we are going through an economic transition.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Trade has been slowing and our local workforce growth is nearing its limits.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As the Finance Minister noted in the Budget Statement, many developed economies going through the same transition have seen their annual gross domestic product growth decelerate to 1% or lower.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Against the backdrop of this new normal and, given the growing requirements in areas, such as healthcare and infrastructure, it seems that the current fiscal climate is one of prudence.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Finance Minister noted that with our spending needs increasing, the Government must continue to spend judiciously, emphasise value-for-money and drive innovation in delivery.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Every Ministry has a part to play in ensuring prudent spending in order to better prepare for the future.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, we observe that in the area of defence and security, regional countries' defence spending is at its highest ever.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We also observe that the countries in our region will continue to increase the defence spending at even faster rates than the rest of the world in the years ahead.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our security environment is increasingly complex and unpredictable.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I recognise that MINDEF must still invest in the necessary resources to ensure that SAF is able to defend Singapore and Singaporeans against different threats to our security.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can MINDEF elaborate on how it remains prudent whilst still ensuring that SAF has the resources it needs to keep Singapore safe and secure?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Vikram Nair, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Most recently, the acquisition of Paya Lebar Air Base was announced.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I have fond memories of Paya Lebar Air Base because my mother was a psychologist there and I used to go there as a child.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: That camp will probably not be there in a few years' time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The camp where I did my NS, Nee Soon Camp, will probably not be functioning as a Basic Military Training (BMT) camp anymore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In fact, I think it has already stopped functioning as one.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Bit by bit, we see a long list of training areas and camps that SAF used to use being given up.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Whether it is the Air Force, Navy or Army, all three services require land to train.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Given local land scarcity and increasing demand for land for other uses, how will SAF ensure that our soldiers receive the necessary training?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: As I mentioned earlier, this is also our 50th Anniversary of NS.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Not only is it a fundamental part of our national defence, it is also an important part of our national identity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: It is the one basis on which men easily relate to one another; and women can easily relate to one another as well talking about what men go through.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: One of the fundamental issues we face with NS is our declining population, and cohorts are likely to get smaller and smaller each year.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Each NSman will, therefore, become even more precious.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: What step is MINDEF taking to ensure that each NSman receives adequate training, his potential is well used and whatever capabilities he has will be well maximised?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Related to this are the new form of threats we face.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Many of the earlier speakers have alluded to the threat faced by cyberattacks, hybrid warfare, and these threats are likely to become even more important in future.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: We will need to develop our capabilities to defend against cyberattacks and, potentially, even to use them as part of a counterattack in a broader defence strategy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: But dealing with this threat also requires people, and the skills required for this are highly specialised and the people with those skills are likely to be few.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: What are the recommendations from the Committee on the Future Economy in relation to this?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: It suggested using NSmen to boost our pool of cyber talent to deal with such threats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I understand that other countries, such as Israel, also use national servicemen to deal with cybersecurity threats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Can MINDEF provide details on whether it plans to implement these suggestions from the Committee on the Future Economy and, if so, how it plans to do so?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Minister Ng spoke of the contributions of our Pioneer Generation of NSmen, noting that, in their time, "Singapore was threatened by Konfrontasi, the communist insurgency in Malaya and the possible fallout from the Vietnam War".

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: When it was first started, NS was essential for the defence of a young nation.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Our Pioneer Generation of NSmen was tasked with defending Singapore at a time when there was barely an SAF to speak of.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Fifty years on, our region has benefited from several decades of relative peace and stability.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: We have a strong and capable SAF that has protected Singapore's borders and interests.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Around the world, other countries, such as Lithuania, France and Sweden, have ended conscription, but, more recently, some are thinking of bringing it back.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Against this backdrop, what role does NS play for Singapore and is it still as important?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: How does MINDEF continuously remind people, including would-be enlistees, NSFs, NSmen, as well as their families, employers and the public at large, of the evolving role but continued importance of NS?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hybrid warfare is a military concept that involves using conventional weapons and unconventional tools, such as economic sanctions and communications, to achieve victory without resorting to open war.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Therefore, we need to review our training doctrines and outcomes to develop new capabilities in our defence force.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Besides training our NSFs and regular Servicemen on new capabilities, we also need to develop a training roadmap to upgrade the capabilities of our NSmen.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, develop fighting capabilities in built-up areas for urban warfare; second, develop information and communications capabilities to counter cyberattacks; and third, develop attack capabilities to deter or destroy any aggressors to our country.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: This Committee was made up of members from diverse backgrounds, including Members of this House, all tasked with reviewing how NS could be strengthened to better serve Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Can MINDEF provide an update on the vocational interest initiative?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Are there other ways in SAF that are being reviewed to better deploy its Servicemen?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: It is the cornerstone of Singapore's defence and security.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: For many Singaporean men, it is a rite of passage where he leaves the comforts of his home at the young age of 18 and takes on the commitment of defending his country, family and friends.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Men, regardless of social status, race or religion, train hand in hand, look out for one another and overcome challenging tasks as one people.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: This "social glue" that is forged through NS is, indeed, a precious outcome for the country.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Given that NSmen give their time to train and defend this nation, it would be right for MINDEF to improve the NS experience.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: How have MINDEF done this over the years and are there recent initiatives to improve NSmen's engagement and fulfilment?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: The NS Orbat (Order of Battle) is understandably different because its mission is different from the civilian sector, and we draw the entire cohort of men from the civilian sector.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: However, to the extent that we can match the private sector interest of the NSmen to their NS vocation, MINDEF will get more out of them, and they more out of NS.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Given the importance of our NSmen to Singapore, we, no doubt, should recognise their contributions and efforts.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: In fact, we should go further and also recognise those who supported them through NS ‒ parents, spouses, girlfriends and so forth.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: I am all for SAF Reservists Association (SAFRA) membership recognition and for also highlighting NS contributions to their employers.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: I think that has gone a long way to recognising them.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: But as for monetary rewards, I am ambivalent.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: We ought to strike the right balance, lest we reduce NS duty to a mere commercial transaction.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Can the Minister highlight what other NS recognition programmes and how else we can do to make NS more fulfilling for our NSmen?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As I was listening to them, I had generally two reactions.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: One, I am thankful that we have even helped some people improve their marksmanship.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We will take credit where credit is due and even when it is not sometimes.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I am thankful for the support across the aisles.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Whether you are of any political affiliation, Non-Constituency Member, Nominated Member ‒ I am very thankful that the support for defence is across all parties.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In fact, I could agree with everything, almost all points brought up by Members of Parliament (MPs).

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And if you listen to their speeches, it was a tour de force of the changing security environment − how the world is, indeed, unpredictable; how new threats are on the horizon and even upon us.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And yet, because we are under pressure with other increased needs, how can SAF and Singapore respond to these threats with the budget allocated?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, there is total agreement with what the Members said.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Their speeches capture the essence of the new security environment for which Singapore and Singaporeans must, indeed, prepare for, and which SAF must adapt to, to protect our sovereignty and defend our home.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Cedric Foo and Dr Teo Ho Pin spoke about this.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Even as we laud their individual contributions, I agree with Members here that SAF must now undertake critical steps to better protect Singapore in this new security environment.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Major parts of my speech will focus on this.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I agree with Members here that the world, indeed, is at an inflexion point.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Interview any world leader now and he will say so.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Even if world leaders do not say so, our citizens can feel that turbulence, that change to come.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The last 25 years after the Cold War were marked by rapid globalisation and relative peace despite the threat of extremist terrorism, which we do not underplay.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This relative peace was so much so that militaries in the European Union (EU) physically downsized.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I remember when I visited Germany, when I first went to their Ministry of Defence, the Bundeswehr was talking about a one-third reduction, a significant reduction.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They wanted to reap the peace dividend of a united Europe against what was perceived to be a declining Russia.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In Asia, it was a good three decades.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: That era we are witnessing is now changing trajectory, as the benefits of globalisation have not been uniform either within or across countries.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And the so-called "ills" of globalisation related to migration and job disruption have eroded popular support in many countries, never mind the benefits of hundreds of millions lifted out of poverty.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, instead of the optimism and hope that greeted the end of the Cold War, uncertainty prevails today.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: There is uncertainty about what "America First" means for global leadership and trade, especially if the erstwhile or current global leader of global trade is not part of the Trans-Pacific Partnership; uncertainty in Asia about how the US-China strategic rivalry will impact Asia and us, as many Members have said before me, especially the pressure on small states like Singapore to choose sides.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Across Europe, still reeling from the global economic crisis in 2008, there is uncertainty about the security threat against some of its members.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Many Members have mentioned Sweden, not just one state but across Europe.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: There is even concern over the existence of EU itself, especially when far-right parties that push for the equivalent of Brexit are gaining ground.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Many Members here have reflected these uncertainties, including Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef, who asked whether we were vulnerable.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And we should accept that the geopolitics will be turbulent and that Singapore has to prepare for choppy waters.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But at the same time, our national strategy to deal with this uncertainty is still sound.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is a simple strategy, one based, firstly, on a strong SAF supported by Total Defence, which we have, with your support, steadily invested resources into every year.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Some Members, including Mr Pritam Singh, have asked what our relations are with our immediate neighbours, and I will tell you that, generally, they are excellent and, indeed, we cooperate on many fronts.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Malacca Straits Patrol, as was mentioned, marked its 10th anniversary last year.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: There continues to be solid support for FPDA, now into its 46th year.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The 18-nation ADMM-Plus has made good progress, with many working groups dealing with different security challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked whether we should have more platforms for cooperation.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Anything that improves military-to-military cooperation, we will undertake.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But we have to understand that, in some aspects, we wait to be invited, for example, the new Sulu Seas Patrols.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have already availed our resources from our Information Fusion Centre in Changi Naval Base to the Sulu Seas Patrols, because that is part of our interest.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our bilateral relations with China and India have also grown.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In 2014, Members will remember that General Chang Wanquan and I agreed on a "Four Point Consensus" in which we affirmed principles and substantive steps to strengthen our bilateral defence cooperation.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For India, Minister Manohar Parrikar and I also signed the revised DCA in 2015 and we are now exploring stepping up collaboration in areas, such as maritime security and counterterrorism.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These strong partnerships stand us in good stead but, ultimately, it is the Next Generation SAF's primary mission and responsibility to deal with security threats in this 21st century, as Members here have said.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We know that it is fully in our court, that SAF must stand ready.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And I agree with Members that this includes the threat of cyberattacks and fake news.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Two years ago, I brought up the issue of hybrid warfare in the Committee of Supply (COS) debates.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It was not a very much bandied word; in fact, it was a very uncommon word.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But today, as I listened to Members' speeches, it has become so common, so well-known only within a short space of two years.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I just came back from the Munich Security Conference and, there, Chancellor Merkel stated openly that some countries considered hybrid warfare to be legitimate.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Last week, the Financial Times had a full write-up on cyber warfare.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They quoted the Russian Defence Minister, "Propaganda must be smart, literate and effective," he told the Lower House of Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This is the head of a government − the German government − saying that there are countries around them which consider this legitimate.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Defence ministers coming out openly to say that "This is part of my Orbat and part of my mission." There is doctrine, there is training, there is execution.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Russia is not alone, as other countries, too, have been reported to have cyber battalions, even cyber divisions in their military and ministries.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And I agree completely with Members here that the Next Generation SAF needs to prepare for this environment where state-orchestrated cyber and information campaigns against another state are not only considered legitimate but can be ongoing all the time.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The impact of that threat can have real and damaging physical consequences.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Estonia is a small nation with about 1.3 million people.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They want to do this and store it in another location, a secret location, in the United Kingdom or Luxembourg.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: At least, they have given you the two places they want to store the information.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Suppose somebody burrows into our Central Provident Fund records, death and registry records, housing records and demolishes them.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: There will be utter chaos for any nation.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Even elections can be influenced by orchestrated cyberattacks.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Democratic National Committee was hacked in the last US Presidential Elections, with thousands of documents released by unknown sources meant to discredit its candidate.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Financial Times alleged that the Russians have already compromised the servers of political parties in France and Germany which are going to have elections.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I do not know how the Financial Times knows this, but they have reported it.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Nearer to home, Members mentioned Indonesia, that it did, indeed, inflame ethnic and political tensions.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And Indonesia has responded by establishing an agency to counter cybercrime and fake news.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our best defence against this information warfare is Total Defence, which has stood the test of time.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I will leave it to Senior Minister of State Maliki to elaborate how we need to update and refresh Total Defence in response to these hybrid threats.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But modern militaries can no longer choose to ignore these external threats through the digital front.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We will be silly to do so and be derelict in our responsibility.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Plans for this speech were prepared before we detected that breach.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is no revelation when I tell Members that we can expect more such cyberattacks in the future.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Indeed, it was that potential of the cyber threat which was recognised early, which is why, even from inception, for SAF, our classified and operational networks were separated from the Internet since we had those systems.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But the threat is now material and even greater.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I agree completely with Members that SAF will need to step up its cyber defences, even as the level of this threat increases.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Cedric Foo asked pointedly about our efforts to combat these new threats.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This new cyber command will be led by a Deputy Secretary.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It will comprise four major formations, each commanded by at least a Colonel or flag officer, a General or an Admiral, within MINDEF and SAF.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The cyber command will oversee policies, train cyber units to monitor and defend our networks 24/7 from threats, which will assess vulnerabilities, detect attempted intrusions and breaches in the system.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: SAF must keep up with the tactics and operations of aggressors in the cyber realm, something which Member Teo Ho Pin spoke about, and because this is a never-ending game, as we do in conventional warfare.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This is a significant build-up from the current numbers and it reflects the importance of this new battlefront.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In response to Members, this is a clear signal.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: NSmen − some Members have asked − yes, NSmen will also be trained in vocations for cyber defence.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It will be silly for us not to; they are our main resource.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And just as security troopers now physically protect key installations, we will deploy these NS cyber defenders to protect our installations together with CSA.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung will elaborate on this.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Some Members like Ms Jessica Tan have asked about technology and how we will deploy resources.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: There is no running away from it, especially so for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As Members have rightly pointed out, we will see a fall in manpower, and our defence technology organisations will gear up to support these changes.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Vikram Nair asked about our STEM recruitment efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The pinnacle Public Service Commission Scholarship (Engineering) within MINDEF will be awarded this year.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Two new labs will be set up so that we can focus our efforts, just as many Members talked about leveraging technology, which I completely agree with.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: One lab will be DSO's, which will set up the robotics lab.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We are at the front edge of this, and it is not as if you can buy commercial software easily, so you will have to invest in resources to kickstart the process.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Six Singapore Infantry Regiment soldiers are currently experimenting with unmanned aerial and ground vehicles to perform their missions.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Navy is putting Unmanned Surface Vehicles (USVs) which can navigate and avoid collisions autonomously into operations.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: SAF, working with the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), has already deployed and developed countermeasures against potential drone attacks.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This is something that Member Joan Pereira asked about.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We are monitoring these aspects, such as developments in Iraq and Syria.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But we are not taking it lightly and, in fact, this is an issue that was discussed at the Security Policy Review Committee that is chaired by Deputy Prime Minister Teo.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And whether you know it or not, in the last National Day Parade that was held at the National Stadium, these systems were already deployed, not only to detect, but countermeasures.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Laws, as you will remember, were also recently enacted by this House and legislation gazetted so that we can have powers.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Analytics and AI Lab will exploit the mega volumes of realtime information that can be derived from the Internet of Things and platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have many platforms, and I agree with Members that not only are we vulnerable, but we need to exploit it.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Every single day, there are about 1,500 commercial ships that ply our waters.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Singapore Maritime Crisis Centre uses a particular programme with AI embedded to generate unique signatures for each of these vessels in our waters.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These individual signatures are collated from multiple sources, which include social media and other specific information.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They are collated, scanned, made sense of and fused to give one picture.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This AI-embedded method detected a possible ISIS supporter on board a tanker that was in our waters in 2015.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, among all the ships, among the tens and hundreds of thousands of occupants, cargo, they detected a possible ISIS supporter.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: That person was barred from disembarking into Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Finding this needle in a big haystack is only possible through modern means.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I also believe that Singapore can take the lead in defence technology even though we are small.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, to achieve that aspiration, DSTA, together with our national universities and the Agency for Science, Technology and Research and Government agencies like GovTech, CSA, the National Research Foundation and the Economic Development Board, will host an inaugural Singapore Defence Technology Summit in 2018.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I asked staff whether there were any global technology summits in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They said, "It does not exist yet", and I replied, "Oh, that is good.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Let us try." This summit will provide a global platform to invite luminaries, leading figures, to come share their views.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It will give us a window into the future.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Not only that; it will allow us opportunities to network and increase our access to ideas and innovation.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Because you and I know that, for defence, for us, it is existential.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We need to deploy technology because other factors are working against us.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We all know that we have finite land and we are building training facilities overseas, such as in Australia, when we signed the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But at the same time, we must have world-class training facilities here.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Vikram Nair talked about his childhood memories and how each time certain camps are taken away.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: There is finite land, we understand the pressures.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Many of the Members here who have done NS will be familiar with the SAF Training Institute (SAFTI) Live Firing Area.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: You and I remember charging up Peng Kang Hill, for whatever reasons we were told to, and being trained at Fighting On Fortified Objective (FOFO), the fortified hill.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But the SAFTI Live Firing Area was built in the 1960s, or 50 years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As Members here pointed out, SAF has changed, cities have changed, terrains have changed, the world has changed.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Members here asked: "How is SAF going to respond to this?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The answer to all your questions is yes.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Not only these, we will need training grounds that reflect the missions and operations that SAF will be called upon to conduct.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But, with your permission, Madam, I think it is easier for Members to see what we are going to build.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Many details but let me give Members the broad gist.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will, therefore, have both urban and conventional terrain.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the urban setting, low houses and high-rise buildings.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the open terrain, jungles, hills and rivers to cross.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But the signature change, because we are using technology, will be state-of-the-art training simulation technologies designed into the operating environment.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are building it from scratch, so that we can do it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There will be interactive targets and battlefield effects, such as artillery attacks, so that our soldiers can train more realistically and get ample feedback about how well they perform.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: When it is completed, SAFTI City will take our NS training to a much higher level of realism and effectiveness.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For instance, for our soldiers who are involved in Island Defence operations, this SAFTI City will allow them to train in mock-up petrochemical complexes, warehouses, container parks and industrial buildings.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Sector 2 will also include urban rubble for Disaster Relief Operations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the areas surrounding SAFTI City, three new Instrumented Battle Circuits (iBACs) will be built.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These will help small units train up their fighting skills because there will be video cameras, data analytics to point to what a specific person did or did not do and they will give feedback on each soldier's performance.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Different scenarios can be configured for both peace time contingency and conventional military operations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Ms Low Yen Ling asked how SAF is going to meet its needs with prudent defence spending, and she is absolutely right.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are aware of these budgetary pressures from an ageing society, coupled with slower growth rates for the economy.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As I have sketched out to Members here, all these new programmes will need significant and sustained resources over the medium term.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will take us 10, 15 or maybe even 20 years to fully size up the Next Generation SAF.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we will reprioritise programmes to meet these challenges that we must face.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Here, I am very thankful for Members who have supported us over the years, steadily, so that we can spend steadily on our defence budgets to renew our Orbat and platforms continually, which today allows us to grow for these new areas, which we did not foresee 10-15 years ago.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Army's refurbished Leopard tanks and Terrexes are young.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Belrex Protected Combat Support Vehicle was introduced last year.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The next-generation Armoured Fighting Vehicle will be rolled out in 2019.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Air Force will upgrade its F-16s with new radars and weapons later this year, and the Aster 30 missile system will be deployed to strengthen our air defences.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Navy has new Littoral Mission Vessels and will need to replace two of its Archer Submarines.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We will announce the replacement for these submarines later this year.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have been able to do this because, every year, we commit a sizeable proportion to defence spending, but steadily.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Member Low Yen Ling made a very incisive comment that in our region, Asia's military spending has outstripped that of the EU and has an average growth of 5.4%.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our 3%-4% is below that, but because we have had a longer runway of steady spending, we can keep to the 3%-4% projection.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But MINDEF will not hesitate to push for higher spending if there are increasing new demands or if the security environment deteriorates.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: MINDEF and SAF are conscious that the Government, with the strong support of Singaporeans, invests substantially into the defence budget each year.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I want to thank Members and Singaporeans for their constant support and I promise you that we will pledge to stretch each defence dollar to the fullest.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Where we can, we will cut cost, as some Members have asked.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: NSmen here will know that we fire blanks for various reasons.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But someone thought, why have blanks, why not have a magazine that can simulate the blank?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These measures, big and small, reflect the culture of prudence, using innovation to cut costs without loss of effectiveness for SAF.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: SAF will develop next-generation capabilities to deal with threats in both the real world and cyberspace.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I want to end with a quote from Dr Goh Keng Swee in his last major public speech.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He said: "The most dependable guarantee of our Independence is a strong SAF.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: A strong SAF, in turn, depends on the political will to make the effort and pay the price." I think Dr Goh's reminder is timeless.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Since the enlistment age of 18 also coincides with the age at which smoking is legally permitted, SAF's role in addressing smoking concerns is, therefore, a natural one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Although smoking prevalence has decreased in Singapore, the proportion of our male population who are smokers is higher than that in many developed countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Although I am not aware of any confirmed evidence, the high proportion of males who smoke happens to coincide with anecdotes suggesting that smoking is still highly prevalent among our Servicemen.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If true, this would have severe consequences across a range of domains, including healthcare costs and discipline.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The tolerance for smoking as a popular culture within armed services is nothing new and it was even embraced in early popular culture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: However, in the context of a modern SAF, it should be viewed as antithetical for many reasons.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If the existing bans on smoking in army camps and training areas are not strongly enforced, they could reduce training effectiveness, lead to an erosion of discipline and have potential knock-on effects on performance in the field for combat personnel.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: There are also the potential difficulties faced by non-smokers if a tolerance of a smoking culture persists in the ranks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, if smoke breaks are permitted, what do non-smokers do?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Although military bases and training areas are off-limits, there is an observable practice of service personnel as well as visitors who gather and smoke outside of camps.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This suggests that while smoking controls may be in place, a smoking culture persists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: What I am pushing for are clear guidelines so that a culture of indiscipline associated with smoking does not arise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: However, I strongly urge SAF to take active steps to ensure smoking rates are not inadvertently allowed to increase.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Even though one would not expect SAF to take it upon itself to eliminate smoking, it should develop strategies to encourage Servicemen who smoke to give up the habit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In doing so, I would caution that it should set realistic targets in consultation with experts in the field of smoking addiction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It should also actively discourage Servicemen from gathering in groups to smoke as, say, a form of social interaction.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Yet, often during my interactions with my residents, the subject of safety during NS training comes up, usually from the mothers and grandmothers with sons and grandsons in NS.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: They have trust in MINDEF but cannot help but worry a little.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: They worry about their sons' and grandsons' health, physical training, the terrains and handling of weapons.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Some unfortunate incidents in the past also serve as reminders of how things could go wrong.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: SAF has consistently reiterated its commitment to safety over the years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe that this is meant to assist to defray their transport costs, given their limited NS allowance.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For NSmen, not all NS units have a "stay in" policy during their In-Camp Training (ICT).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of these NSmen may still be required to book out very late or book in very early due to the demands of their roles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In last year's COS debate, Minister Ong Ye Kung mentioned that students in local universities are called up for Operationally Ready NS (ORNS) training while studying.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are full-time students and may be no different from NSF personnel in that they are not working and do not have income.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister to consider allowing this benefit to NSmen who are full-time students studying private courses and NSmen who are unemployed at the time of ICT.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Their commanders can help administer such claims in accordance with suitable conditions to be stipulated by MINDEF.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe that allowing such transport claims will assist some of our NSmen to cope with booking out and booking in at odd hours without having to shoulder any unnecessary financial burden.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: One of the Committee on the Future Economy (CFE) initiatives was to "Acquire and Utilise Deep Skills", which can apply to people serving NS as well.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: In 2015, MINDEF and MHA, together with the Singapore Workforce Development Agency, jointly organised the Career Skills Workshop for all NSFs.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: This arose from the recommendation by the Committee to Strengthen National Service and aims to help NSFs transit to the workforce after they complete full-time NS.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Can MINDEF elaborate on what other initiatives are planned to prepare our NSFs for life after NS?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: He said that, and I quote, "While Singaporeans are confident that our home and our way of life are safeguarded by an advanced and highly trained SAF, we must know that our security agencies cannot do the job on their own." Last year, I spoke with great concern of the threat to Singapore posed by ISIS and by terrorism more generally during the COS debate in 2016.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In the past 12 months, it appears that the news headlines have become even more troubling.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Recent developments have also shed light on a variety of other non-traditional threats to our security.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For example, countless cyberattacks around the globe have had serious real-world outcomes.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Countries or groups have hacked political parties and institutions with the intent of influencing political outcomes.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Cyberattackers have also proven their ability to hack into bank accounts by the thousands and to steal unsuspecting victims of hard-earned money.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We have also learnt of cyber breaches closer to home where personal information has been stolen.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Some cyberattacks can be attributed to criminals and mischief makers but the fact that there are people out there with the skills to hurt us through attacks in cyberspace should worry us.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Put in the wrong hands, cyberattackers can be trained and employed to wage bigger conflicts against Singapore as a whole.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: At the same time, we have learnt how countries and groups with malicious intent can use influence campaigns to divide and damage communities as well.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: It is clear that a military solution alone cannot address the wide-ranging security challenges that Singaporeans faced.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Even the US, which spends more on its military than the next few countries combined, has been a target of large-scale cyberattacks and influence campaigns.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Experts argued that the conflict between countries will increasingly be fought in the grey zone between war and peace, where military forces may not be even involved.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This means that ordinary citizens could be on the front line of hybrid attacks against Singapore.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We have all heard from Minister Ng Eng Hen earlier.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: He spoke about how some countries even see mounting hybrid warfare as legitimate.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, in light of all these recent developments, can MINDEF provide its assessment on how hybrid threats have continued to evolve and how we are strengthening total defence to deal with these threats?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What are some challenges and constraints in implementing the remaining proposals?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: At the COS debate last year, we learnt that our younger generation, unlike the Pioneers, saw events, such as Konfrontasi, racial riots and our road to Independence, as study subjects rather than personal experience or memories.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: With that in mind, I would like to ask how MINDEF is working to engage our younger generations of Singaporeans on defence issues and to foster a strong commitment to defence amongst the youth.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: I note that Senior Minister of State Maliki had launched a "Commitment to Defence" Ambassadors programme to allow SAF Pioneers to engage and inspire the younger generation.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: While we may no longer be in the era of World War II or Konfrontasi, Singapore still faces multifaceted threats to our security.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: Just in the past year alone, developments from around the world and the region have shown us that threats to our way of life, including from terrorism, cyberattacks and fake news, have become increasingly apparent and are closer to us than we think.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: More so than ever, the security challenges of today require the vigilance, unity and resilience not just of SAF and the Home Team, but of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: In light of our rapidly evolving security environment, can we have a status update on MINDEF's Total Defence efforts and how it fits in with other Government efforts, such as SG Secure?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Every year, Total Defence Day is observed on 15 February to commemorate the day when Singapore fell to the Japanese in World War II in 1942.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Since 1984, a wide range of activities has been organised to remind Singaporeans of the roles they can play in building a strong nation and defending Singapore.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: The five pillars of Total Defence, namely, military defence, civil defence, economic defence, social defence and psychological defence, provide a framework to guide Singaporeans to play a part in Total Defence.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Many Singaporeans still do not know their roles in the five pillars of Total Defence.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: The operational readiness of Singaporeans in Total Defence is also lacking.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Both the young and old Israelis are ready to respond to any attacks on their land.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: In fact, when I was there, I saw a group of youths armed with rifles patrolling the streets of the city centre.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Thus, I would urge MINDEF to make Total Defence real and drive the fighting spirit of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Last month, I was in Pulau Tekong for the launch of NS50 − the 50th Anniversary of NS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Enlistees were there on their first day, together with their families, and I joined them for lunch at the cookhouse.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I asked "Is this standard fare?" They assured me that it is like that every day, but it is not chicken every day.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is a standard that has been kept up.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I sat with many of the enlistees and their families, spoke to them, asked them if they were ready and how they felt.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I sensed amongst the youngsters pride, even eagerness.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many of them shaved their heads and then get enlisted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Though the hairstyle, of shaving your heads, both inside and outside camp, is actually similar.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But they were quite eager to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I asked the parents how they felt and they all said, every single one, NS is good for their sons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One key reason is that we see how NS has bonded us all together and toughened up our young.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Another important reason is that after 50 years, fathers have gone through NS and know its benefits and now are supportive of their sons going through the same experience.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is truly a duty passing from one generation to the next.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, I will talk about how we can better leverage our most precious resource in SAF − NSmen, and how we can enhance the NS experience.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Minister for Defence Dr Ng Eng Hen has spoken about a Next Generation SAF, one where we have to maximise the talent, expertise and contribution of every single Serviceman.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This centre will focus on fitness regimes, soldier nutrition, prehabilitation regimes to prevent injuries, and rehabilitation to help injured Servicemen recover.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The centre will also integrate training packages on resilience to enhance the mental strength of our soldiers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan asked how SAF addresses smoking in SAF.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are aligned with national policy on this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will continue to encourage Servicemen to maintain a healthy lifestyle and reduce their health risk factors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, smoking is not allowed in SAF camps and bases, except at designated smoking points.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Cigarettes are not sold in any of our camps or bases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We also partner the Health Promotion Board to conduct smoking cessation workshops for our Servicemen.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But soldiers will need to take personal responsibility for their own health, too.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, we maximise contributions of NSmen by deploying them better.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Technological advancements in SAF have altered the nature of vocations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For certain vocations, automation has greatly reduced the physical demands.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the past, Combat Engineers had to lift and hold heavy interlocking parts of a bridge.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, these bridges have been replaced with the Mobility 3rd Generation bridge, or M3G.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: M3G is deployed through a remote interface with the help of a hydraulic arm.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In other words, you can now deploy a bridge that can carry up to three five-tonner trucks, mainly by pushing buttons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because of these advancements, we have been reviewing vocation requirements and can better deploy our NSFs effectively in accordance with their fitness and abilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Third, we take into account the vocational interest of enlistees and, in so doing, better match skills and interests with deployment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Lee Yi Shyan asked about the vocational interest initiative, and Mr Cedric Foo asked how NS can be made more engaging and fulfilling and better recognised by society.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have implemented the Vocation Interest initiative to promote greater personal ownership by NSFs over their NS experience.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Their indicated interest will be an additional factor in determining their vocations, together with other considerations, such as suitability, manpower and operational requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is some perception that enlistees, fresh out of school, when asked to indicate their vocational preference, will avoid the very "siong" vocations like Infantry and Guards, and then they will pick non-combat vocations that are more related to their areas of studies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They know that the training is "siong" but good for them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will develop a new cyber vocation in support of the new cyber command, which Minister Ng has announced.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This vocation will allow SAF to tap on the talent available to defend our military networks and systems.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our cyber defenders will need to possess a high level of skill, given the increasing frequency and complexity of cyberattacks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They will be entering a very selective and demanding vocation, comparable to the Commandos or Naval Divers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As part of their duties, they will also be supporting CSA in a pilot scheme to defend our critical information infrastructure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Pre-enlistees who possess these skills will be rigorously selected and identified, possibly through established local cyber competitions, camps and activities, as well as rigorous selection tests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I expect many of these competitions and selection will be done in our education institutions − junior colleges, Institutes of Technical Education and polytechnics.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The impact is not just on the few selected for the vocation but will heighten the interest and expertise in cyber and digital technology across the student masses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This will also increase the talent pool for national defence as well as Singapore's growing cyber industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our efforts over the years have been guided by the recommendations of CSNS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The first is safety, which is a critical element of training.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked how we can provide assurance that our NSmen will be safe while serving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Every year, 20,000 families entrust their sons and, increasingly daughters, to us.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We take the issue of safety very, very seriously.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We worry about the safety of our Sservicemen as much as their mothers and grandmothers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And this is how we keep our safety record very well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One is to strengthen safety culture at the unit level and another is to further promote open reporting of near-miss incidents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: SAF has accepted the Panel's findings and will improve on these areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: SAF has also been doing more to reassure NSmen's family members and loved ones of our emphasis on safety.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because safety culture must be inculcated at the unit level, outreach must also be done at the unit level.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It makes a special effort to engage NSmen's family members regularly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, upon enlistment, there is a briefing for family members on what this is all about.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the Combat Diving Course graduation ceremony, families are also shown videos of diving training drills plus many other engagements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All these assure parents that while the training programme is tough, it is carried out progressively, professionally and safely.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because the strength of NS as an institution lies in our NSmen, it is important for society to show our appreciation to them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But as we all know and as Mr Cedric Foo has pointed out, vouchers cannot reflect the true value of the commitment and contribution of our Servicemen.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is just a small way for us to say "Thank you".

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Support and appreciation from society are the strongest form of motivation an NSman can receive.

speaker: The Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will encourage this through the NS50 Week in August, where companies and organisations can thank and appreciate the NSmen amongst them.
